text: The firmware emulates a minimal ESPHome native API device (plaintext, TCP 6053) so the user's existing havpe-server (Go, Silero VAD on the server, ElevenLabs STT/TTS, webhook + regex shortcuts) can drive it unchanged. Rejected: a new WebSocket protocol in havpe-server (duplicates a working pipeline, two device protocols to maintain). The device advertises mDNS hostname prefix home-assistant-voice- because havpe-server discovers by that prefix; this is safe only because the user's real Voice PE is no longer in use (two matching devices make the server refuse to start).

Wake word is 'Alexa' via ESP-SR WakeNet9s. The user wanted 'whatever microWakeWord has'; Alexa is the only phrase both microWakeWord and WakeNet9s ship. Running microWakeWord (TFLite Micro) on the ESP32-C6 was rejected: no SIMD/esp-nn acceleration and no FPU on the C6. Silero VAD on the device was rejected for the same reasons plus RAM (about 2 MB float model); end-of-speech detection stays on the server.

Reply audio: havpe-server serves ElevenLabs MP3 plus 44.1/48 kHz WAV tones by URL. The user prefers decoding MP3 on the device (esp_audio_codec). Agreed fallback if RAM does not allow it: change havpe-server to request pcm_16000 from ElevenLabs and serve WAV, so the device only decodes WAV. The user pre-approved this fallback.
Builds use the espressif/idf:v5.5.3 Docker image instead of a local ESP-IDF install (the user's machine only has an old IDF 4.4 environment). v5.5.3 matches Waveshare's examples.

The board lives on the user's main network (192.168.10.x, same subnet as havpe-server at 192.168.10.4), not the IoT VLAN. The IoT VLAN (192.168.13.x) blocks new connections from the board to the main LAN, which broke fetching reply audio from havpe-server's HTTP port 8085; the API connection only worked because the server opens it. The user gave the board a fixed IP (192.168.10.206) and points havpe-server at it; mDNS discovery also works on this subnet.

The user decided KEY (GPIO10) mutes and unmutes the microphone instead of starting a voice session; the wake word is the only session trigger. Mute fully releases the microphone (privacy, like the Voice PE mute switch). A press during a session takes effect when the session returns to idle. Mute state is not persisted: the board always boots unmuted.

The user accepts GPL for this firmware and prefers AGPL. So GPLv3 code from ESPHome (micro_wake_word C++) may be reused for the planned microWakeWord port; the project licence should be AGPL-3.0 (GPLv3 code can be combined into an AGPLv3 work).

Face screen decisions from the user: only 8 faces (idle_default, listening, thinking, speaking, muted, blink, idle_happy_eyes, idle_curious) out of a 21-face set; the rest stay out of the repo. Plain black background (AMOLED power and burn-in). Burn-in protection: the user pointed out that a few-pixel drift leaves eye centres always lit, so the agreed measures are idle dimming (about 25% after 30 s idle, full during sessions) plus a slow ±20 px drift, blink and short variety faces. Rejected: alpha-only (A8) tinted images (lose the pink accents), compressed LVGL images (need full RAM decode), a separate flash partition (not needed once the set is small).

The user's real goal is one custom wake word phrase; the engine does not matter. WakeNet cannot do this in practice (Espressif trains custom WakeNet models only as a paid service or on request, weeks of turnaround), so microWakeWord replaces WakeNet if it runs fast enough on the C6. The earlier rejection (gaznrt) was based on 'no FPU', which matters little because microWakeWord models are int8 and its feature frontend is fixed-point; the open question is only inference speed without SIMD. Agreed 2026-11-08: one model only, no VAD model, no 'stop' model, .tflite embedded in the app with EMBED_FILES.

Faces move from PNG images to shapes drawn by code (user request, 2026-11-08). The design source is the user's 'Cute robot faces.html' (Claude artifact bundle, kept out of the repo): five state faces in the 'glow pills' style (idle, listening, thinking, speaking, muted), plus 'happy arcs' and 'big shiny eyes' as the two idle variety faces. 'Sleepy' was not used. User decisions: keep the plain black background, not the design's #151225 (the black-background decision in jwxjvv still holds). No glow, because LVGL shadows apply only to filled shapes and the blur is computed again on every repaint. All of the design's animations are kept, including a muted blink. The listening head tilt is faked with opposite vertical eye offsets, because rotation needs an off-screen layer that does not fit in RAM. Rejected: a stadium or ellipse-mask approximation of the old PNG faces (replaced by the new design).

Outcome 2026-11-08: microWakeWord runs on the C6. The custom 'Stavrobot' model measured about 3.6 ms average inference per 20 ms period (stride 2) and cost about 12.6 KB more idle minimum heap than WakeNet9s. WakeNet and ESP-SR were removed. This overturns the 'too slow on the C6' part of gaznrt; the Silero VAD rejection in gaznrt still stands.

Blink timing was tuned by the user watching the panel (2026-11-08): the HTML design's 120 ms close / 200 ms open looked too slow and 3 to 7 s felt slightly too frequent, so it is 90 ms close / 160 ms open every 4 to 8 s. A two-frame (open/closed) blink was rejected as looking wrong.

Conversation screen decisions from the user (2026-11-08), from 'Cute robot faces.html': layout C (boards C1 thinking and C2 speaking a long answer). C1 and C2 show the user's transcript in an outlined italic bubble at the top right, above the robot's bubble. An earlier plan dropped the transcript only because the architect misread the design. Rejected layouts: A (face above text), B (heard text above, reply below), D (caption strip), E (transcript with mini face). Thinking and speaking-with-text use the conversation screen. The full-size thinking face is dropped. A reply with no text keeps the full-size speaking face. After a reply the bubbles stay for 2.5 s with a mini idle face. Fonts: DM Sans (SemiBold 26 for the reply, Italic 24 and 18 for the transcript) converted for LVGL, chosen over built-in Montserrat partly so curly quotes, dashes and the ellipsis render. A C1 transcript is capped at 3 lines (user-confirmed assumption).

The design reference 'Cute robot faces.html' is now kept in the repo as docs/cute-robot-faces.html (user request, 2026-11-08), replacing the earlier decision to keep it out. The new version adds 'Surprised (picked up)' and 'Relieved (put down)'. User decisions: the picked-up face is shown while the device moves and the relieved face for 4 s after it is put down (the user first asked for 2 s, then chose 4 s so one full design cycle plays). Both apply only in idle and muted, never during a session or an error. Rejected: QMI8658 hardware motion interrupts, in favour of polling.

The user chose (2026-11-08) to play the Voice PE wake_word_triggered chime at the wake word, overlapping the wait for havpe-server's answer, rather than when the microphone opens. Accepted trade: speech during the ~0.48 s tone is lost (shared I2S bus). Also chosen: the real Voice PE sound trimmed to two notes over a synthesized beep or the full 0.95 s clip, and no tone for the no-server case or for mute, errors or end of speech.

2026-11-08: 'No speech detected' after a clearly spoken 'hello' was diagnosed from the havpe-server log: ElevenLabs returned 'Hello.' about 0.4 s before the 3 s cutoff, but Silero never reached 3 frames at >= 0.35. Cause: Stavvy capture is about 19 dB quieter than the Voice PE; offline, Silero fails on the Stavvy recordings 15 to 20 dB down. The wake chime was ruled out (the capture after it opens at 16 kHz and a session with the chime worked) except that it delays the first audio by about 0.54 s. Fix chosen: +12 dB digital gain on the streamed audio in the firmware. Rejected: gain on the server (hides the device level, affects other devices). Separately, the user took a havpe-server ticket (written by hand, not tracked here) to start the no-speech countdown at the first audio chunk and log the highest Silero probability on failure.
